item.title: 🔵 Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

item.title: 🟠 European supermarkets that failed to act after French freezer attack are now feeling the heat
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday.

The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution.

item.title: 🟠 A compromised DevOps laptop caused the $6.3B Binance breach
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential data exposure — review monitoring and incident-response readiness.

Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers.

“Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization.

item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

A malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace attempted to install a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor on developers’ machines, potentially giving attackers remote access to systems holding source code, credentials and other sensitive information.

“Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace,” Cursor said in a security notice.

Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29.

The company said the malicious code attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable local SSH access, and establish a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server.

item.title: 🟠 Why do we keep testing employees for yesterday’s phishing attacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

“Yesterday’s price is not today’s price,” a phrase Fat Joe popularized in 2021, reminds us that what worked yesterday may not deliver the same value today.

In cybersecurity, this matters when we continue to assess employees against familiar phishing techniques while attackers use AI to craft more convincing, personalized messages. Having conducted multiple phishing simulations and one in October, 2026, I believe we need to ask a harder question: are we preparing people for the phishing attacks they are likely to face today, or testing their ability to recognize or remember the warning signs we have taught them to expect? What happens when those warning signs don’t apply or they face novel attacks?

AI -enabled “phishing landscape”

item.title: 🟠 Who approves the files that control your AI coding assistant?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions.

Before approving it, the reviewer needs to answer a different question: what will this change allow to run on a colleague’s machine?

In an October 8 analysis of agent-skill distribution, StepSecurity revisited the June Miasma campaign, which planted AI-tool and editor configuration in a Microsoft repository without modifying application source. item.title: 🔴 What a security strategy that survives 2027 looks like
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity.

“AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.”

In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment.

“That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says. “It also means expanding how we use AI in our own security operations to handle routine work, so our experts can focus on the threats and initiatives that matter most. item.title: 🔵 Choosing a WAAP in 2026: 3 questions that separate the shortlist
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential budget or licensing impact — verify renewal terms and forecast changes.

One platform or four

Your WAF renewal is coming up. The API team has its own tooling in mind, the fraud team wants a bot product, and someone in networking owns DDoS. Four controls, four consoles, four sets of policies in front of the same applications. That is the situation a Web Application and API Protection platform, or WAAP, exists to replace: one service in front of the application portfolio that handles the WAF, API security, bot management, DDoS, and client-side script protection together.

The category is settled. What changed in 2026 is the evidence. Buyers now have certified test data that measures how well these platforms stop attacks and how often they stop legitimate traffic by mistake, and the two numbers together tell you more than any feature list.

item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

The identity landscape you’re responsible for looks nothing like it did just a few years ago. Employees and contractors now share the enterprise with service accounts, machine identities, and a fast-growing population of AI agents — all accessing business systems and data.

Every one of those identities represents an access decision, and every access decision is now a potential point of accountability that lands on your desk. Regulators and boards want proof. They expect security leaders to show who, or what, has access to critical systems and how that access is being governed.

But when human and nonhuman identities (NHIs) change faster than manual processes can keep up, proof becomes much harder to produce. item.title: 🔵 Why continuous governance, not periodic reviews, is the new standard for identity security
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Continuous identity governance is the operational model that enables organizations to validate access in real time, rather than relying on scheduled reviews to catch problems after they’ve already occurred. It replaces quarterly certifications and annual audits with ongoing visibility, automated policy enforcement, and always-current evidence of who, or what, has access to critical systems.

For CISOs, this shift matters now because the identity landscape has outgrown the tools built to govern it. Employees and contractors now share the environment with service accounts, machine identities, and autonomous AI agents, all requesting access at a pace no manual review cycle can track.  When governance happens only periodically, the gap between review dates becomes an exposure window that boards and regulators increasingly expect security leaders to own.

Why periodic reviews can’t keep up with modern identity environments

item.title: 🔴 Anthropic AI model finds Linux kernel bug that leads to remote root access
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Linux servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) could be vulnerable to remote code execution through a flaw in the kernel’s networking stack.

Anthropic has disclosed a zero-click exploit developed with an unreleased Claude research model that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root, without requiring any user interaction.

Tracked as CVE-2026-98432, the vulnerability is a race-condition-induced use-after-free (UAF) bug in the Linux kernel. Anthropic demonstrated how an attacker could exploit the flaw remotely to leak kernel memory, defeat Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), hijack kernel control flow, and ultimately execute an attacker-controlled shell command.

The research is part of Anthropic’s broader effort to evaluate AI models’ ability to discover and exploit vulnerabilities in widely deployed software. The company disclosed five exploit chains involving Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux to…

“Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release.

Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added.

item.title: 🔴 Everyday channels are available in an incident, but you may not want them
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

The first hours after a serious cyber incident are filled with activity. Security starts investigating, IT works to contain the impact, legal begins assessing potential obligations, and executives want to know what happened and what the company is doing about it. Most teams rely on the same tools they use every day to coordinate that work, which usually means email, Slack, Teams, shared documents and video calls.

Coordination gets much more complicated when the company’s email or collaboration environment is part of the incident. Email may still work, employees may still be able to join meetings, and nothing on the surface may suggest that the organization has lost control of its communications. Meanwhile, an attacker with access to accounts used by responders may read the team’s messages, monitor containment plans or impersonate someone involved in the response.

item.title: 🔵 We are not ready for what AI has done to red teaming
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Something shifted in offensive security over the last eighteen months that most organizations haven’t fully absorbed yet. It isn’t that attackers got smarter. It’s that the economics of attack changed entirely — and those of us who run red teams have had a front-row seat to the transformation.

The conversation about AI in cybersecurity tends to fixate on defense: better anomaly detection, faster triage, and AI-assisted SOC analysts. That framing misses the more urgent story. The attack side of this ledger has already been rewritten. A small, well-equipped offensive team using frontier AI models today can outperform what was possible with a much larger traditional operation just two years ago, by a margin that should unsettle every security leader reading this.

Through our work on the front lines of offensive security, the consensus is clear: if you are not augmenting your operations with AI, you are already at a disadvantage.

item.description:

In May 2017, the WannaCry cryptoworm spread across the internet, compromising more than 200,000 computers in at least 100 countries. The National Audit Office called it the largest cyberattack ever to hit the NHS in England. At least 80 of 236 hospital trusts were infected or disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled, five hospitals diverted ambulances, and more than 1,200 pieces of diagnostic equipment were infected.

What stopped WannaCry was a stroke of luck. A researcher reverse engineered the malware, noticed it contacting a domain nobody had registered, and registered it. item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned of a high severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw that attackers are chaining with PHP2Shell bugs in the wild.

Identified as CVE-2026-46300, it could allow attackers to run malicious code with root permissions, giving them unrestricted ability to run commands, tamper with system settings, view, edit, or delete files, and perform other malicious actions.

Once attackers establish root access, they can perform any action on a server including, but not limited to, disabling the server, creating accounts, removing accounts, connecting to other servers, and adding/removing software, explained Scott Miserendino, CTO at security and compliance platform DataBee.

A high-severity flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) is under active exploitation to crash vulnerable devices.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76418 and rated 8.6 in severity, is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group, Cisco said in its advisory. It could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to send a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN that results in a device reload and thus denial of service.

item.title: 🟠 Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls.

The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions.

“If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote…
